translation:
Volume One

If [the text] were altered, nothing could remain complete without regret; the only reason this [version] stands out above the rest is that it preserves the original intent of the Ishinpo.
Among the various officials of the Song who fixed and edited it, their personal tastes often led to repeated changes in the wording and phrasing.
Scholars of later ages who revised it also did the same; and so the text has already undergone much alteration.
It has been examined quite broadly, and among those who preserve its original form, it is especially esteemed by specialists in medical arts.
As for the lost portions, it is not known how many hundred sections there were, but the Wang family's Waitai Biyao (Arcane Essentials from the Imperial Library) drew upon them.
Now there remain only a few extant family versions, and checking against the bibliographic treatises of the Sui and Tang dynasties,
it is recorded that from the Six Dynasties down through the Tang, the writings of our country's medical arts have survived here.
[Some uncertain text] — recorded in the fifth month of the year hinoto-no-ushi, and now, in the third month of the year kanoe-tatsu, because of this,
passages marked in vermillion ink are those I personally selected while searching through and examining the list of names and the table of contents here.
Those transcribed in blue ink are the annotations made by Master Katsurayama.
My friend Mr. Shima made a shadow-copy for me, following its marginal glosses, and I then
borrowed the thirty fascicles of the Ishinpo by Tanba no Yasuyori from the Taki family, and undertook this compilation and revision.

translation:
Yasuyori compiled this book, drawing on more than a hundred sources, all texts of the Six Dynasties and Tang periods. Moreover, there are dozens of works not recorded in the bibliographic treatises and not listed in the Wang family's catalogue. As for the texts that survive today, their format and wording differ considerably. Note the following:

Since ancient times our court's envoys sent to communicate with Tang China, and the students who studied abroad there, followed one another without interruption for more than two hundred years. The books and records they brought back were, at the time, directly obtained transcriptions kept in the palace storehouses and by court scholars — not works that passed through the hands of artisans and merchants as happened under the Hu and Song dynasties. Yasuyori mainly made use of these, and so, although this text preserves the old form of the original books, it differs somewhat from versions that survive elsewhere. Let me cite one or two examples as proof.

Where it quotes the Qianjin fang, there are passages concerning compounding medicines with specific timing, giving ten prescriptions and three treasures, as well as ancient physicians first seeking a cure for illness before all else — yet the various extant editions of this text have repeatedly been cut and abridged. Comparing them with the authentic original, the Qianjin fang here is fully preserved intact. This chapter, [as found in] the red-sheathed hall's original Qianjin fang, survives only in fragments, though many copies are kept in Zan Province.

As for the transcribed copies that have portions missing, there is also the Soshu text, which according to the general catalogue is considered to be based on Su Jing's Bencao. Its sequence of sections and the enumeration of items correspond with the Zhenglei materia medica. The phrasing retains the character of the Tang period, preserving much that is otherwise lost, of value for elementary study.

For example, characters such as "centipede" written as "Wu Ban" (呉班), or "cat" written for "numbness and pain," and the like; or "tiger" written as "white beast," and "ye" written as "qi" — all such instances can be found. Is this not a treasure to be prized and valued? Hence I have, apart from technical matters, noted here as a kind of marginal secret record my discussion of this book.

As for the lower portion of this work, discussion of it does not go back further than the near-ancient period. The details are recorded in the postface by Master Yōkei, which states that in the Eichō era there was a gap, [and that] the white [text] of Hakuraku-tō (the Yoroku-fuji lineage?) Lord So, after extensive search, could never be recovered, and it was said to have long since been lost.

The Ninna-ji temple's register notes it as secret, so that no one could see it; later, in the year of Boat (gai), it was once again sought as a secret text.

In the year of the Tiger [it was] respectfully retired/stored below.

In the bibliographic catalogue of our court, in the Eikyō era, the year of Kinoto-Hitsuji, the Shogun Minamoto no Yoshinori ordered the Great Scholar Kiyohara no Naritada to compile and record it. It came to be known as the Ninna-ji Temple Catalogue; among its entries listed as "scattered and lost" is this one.

translation:
[The place where] mists and dews gather; its people are fond of sour flavors and eat preserved/fermented foods, and so the people have tight-grained [skin] and a reddish complexion. Their diseases are spasms and numbness (痺), and the proper treatment is fine needling — hence the nine needles came from the south.

The central region: its land is level and damp, and Heaven [and Earth] give rise there to many kinds of things; the people eat a mixed diet and do not toil much. Hence their diseases are mostly wasting, reversal (jue), cold and heat; the proper treatment is guided exercise and massage (daoyin anqiao) — hence [these] came from the center.

Thus the sage combines [these different methods] in treatment, so that each obtains what suits it; thus treatments differ yet the illness is cured in every case — this is because one has grasped the true nature of the disease and understands the great principles of treatment.

It is also said: "Whoever wishes to diagnose illness must always ask whether [the patient] was once honored and later became base. Even if [the illness] is not caused by invading evil, the disease arises from within —

this is called 'Loss of Nourishment' (tuoying). One who was once wealthy and later became poor is said to have 'Lost Essence' (shijing). [...]

Those who have Lost Essence and suffer 'Loss of Nourishment' have been injured; those who have suffered disgrace and loss of fat have been injured. Some, once poor, later became wealthy and honored —

the hardship they once endured, though it did not harm them through external evil, harmed their spirit; such [emotional] suffering can indeed bring about disease."

It is also said: "When illness first arises in the yin, first treat the yin and afterward treat the yang. When it first arises in the yang,

first treat the yang and afterward treat the yin. In every case, first treat the root."

It is also said: "When one is bold and takes pleasure, yet the will is troubled, disease arises [...] in the vessels; treat it with moxibustion and needling. When one is bold and joyful in will and takes pleasure, disease arises

in the fat/membranes; treat it with calming of worry, fear and fright. When the vessels are blocked and do not communicate, disease arises

in the sinews; treat it with guided exercise (daoyin). When one is content in will and given to brooding, when one is bold and takes pleasure in will,

but the will is embittered, disease arises, manifesting as moaning and crying out; treat it with medicines, with [measures against] distress and fright."

translation:
If there is numbness [insensitivity of the flesh], treat it with massage and medicinal liquors.

The text says: illnesses arising from wind, cold, summer-heat, dampness, diet, or sexual excess, which are not disorders of the heart-mind, may be treated with needle and stone.

Decoctions can remove them. But illnesses caused by joy, anger, worry, and brooding that injure the spirit must be treated by reasoning things through, clarifying and settling the patient's temperament, in order to remove them.

When joy, anger, worry, brooding, and desire become overwhelming, one should use needle and medicine together with spiritual counsel (meditation/guidance) to assist the treatment; needle and medicine alone cannot cure it.

[This is what is meant by] "cure it."

It is further said, Bogao stated: "The art of war says, do not meet head-on a force that comes on like a surging drum-roll; do not strike a formation that stands as solid and imposing as a great hall." The method of needling likewise says: do not needle when the heat is blazing hot, do not needle when the sweat is streaming down, do not needle when the pulse is vast and turbulent, and do not needle when the disease and the pulse are working against each other.

The Zhenjiu Jing (Classic of Acupuncture and Moxibustion) says: for children under ten and the elderly over seventy, needling must not be used — only moxibustion and mild, sweet medicines [are permitted].

[One should] break down the great qi, and only afterward settle and calm it with massage.

Thus, when the evil qi is still vigorous, one must not attack it directly; one should wait until it declines.

The Yimen Fang says: the general rule is that in spring and summer it is appropriate to induce sweating by moxibustion.

Generally, when taking decoctions to induce sweating, once the illness responds one should stop; it is not necessary to use up the whole dose.

In general, when inducing sweat, one should let it come on gradually and spread evenly through the body, moistening it all over at once — this is best. However,

when inducing sweat, even if [profuse, one should] not let it stream and drip like pouring rain; instead apply a rubbing powder to the body, and take care not to expose it to wind or cold.

translation:
Whenever there is heavy sweating and the pulse becomes surging and large, as in intermittent fever recurring once a day, induce sweating again; once the sweat comes out, the bowels will ease and the condition will resolve.

Administer Cinnamon Twig and Ephedra Decoction:
Ephedra, 4 liang (nodes removed); Cinnamon heart, 2 liang; Licorice, 1 liang (roasted); Apricot kernel, 80 pieces (tips removed).
Boil in 7 sheng of water: first boil the ephedra until it bubbles, skim off the foam, then add the remaining ingredients and boil down to
2.5 sheng. Divide into three doses, spaced about 7–8 li apart [in time]. After taking, keep covered to bring on sweating again; no congee is needed. The rest follows the method for Cinnamon Twig Decoction.

Cinnamon Twig Method:

Whenever, after sweating has been induced, the sweating continues to leak without stopping, and the patient dislikes wind, has difficulty urinating, and the four limbs feel slightly stiff and hard to move,
treat with Cinnamon Twig Decoction plus Aconite:
Cinnamon heart, 3 liang; Licorice, 2 liang (roasted); Fresh ginger, 3 liang;
Jujube, 12 pieces (split).
Cut the ingredients and boil in 7 sheng of water over a low fire, reducing to 3 small sheng; remove the dregs and divide into three warm doses. Once the decoction has been taken,
shortly after, drink 1 sheng of hot rice congee to assist the medicine's effect; keep warmly covered to bring on sweating. If sweating does not occur, take the dose again
as before. If sweating still does not come, [ ] wait about half a day, until by the next morning one notices its effect, then observe the patient.

If the original symptoms remain, take this decoction again; in some cases, up to three doses may be needed before sweating readily occurs.

"Woman's reins" — this is a separate section.

Thus it is relieved: in the case of the Cinnamon Twig and Aconite Decoction, one additional piece of prepared aconite is added to the decoction.

A text says: "In winter one may apply hot compresses or medicinal fomentation" — ( ) if sweating is induced and sweat appears, with sores developing and vomiting-diarrhea in the mouth, [this is improper].

In cases of strangury (淋家), one must not induce sweating; if sweat is forced out, the eyes will stare fixedly and the patient will be unable to sleep.

In cases of nosebleed (衄家), one must not induce sweating; if sweat is forced out, there will be sinking at the forehead.

When there is blockage in the throat with coughing, one must not induce sweating in such a patient.

After a major purgation, if sweating is then induced, this will cause abdominal distension and fullness.

After sweating has been induced, if the patient feels cold, this indicates deficiency; if the patient does not feel cold but has heat, this indicates excess — in such a case one should harmonize the stomach and nourish the qi.

[Marginal notes]
On Running Piglet Qi (奔豚氣)
Running Piglet patients — origin of the disease, as recorded.
If the lips and tongue are somewhat curled and relaxed,
and a sensation rises from below the navel and rushes up to the heart,
this is due to anxious thought and pent-up qi.

[Heading] Cases in which sweating must not be induced:

In cases of recent severe vomiting and purging, or chest bleeding, or self-exhaustion from blood loss, or after an attack of reversed-flow cough, or in women recently injured by childbirth — in all these, [sweating must not be induced].

In cases of coughing with free urination, or if urinary control is lost, one must not induce sweating; if sweat is forced out, reversed-flow cough will result.

After sweating has been induced, if the patient drinks water excessively, panting will surely result; and if cold water is poured over the body, chronic panting will result.

After sweating has been induced, if the patient feels throbbing below the navel, this indicates an impending attack of Running Piglet Qi; it should be treated with Poria, Cinnamon Heart, Licorice, and Jujube (in large dose).

In cases of sores and ulcers on the body, even though there is bodily pain, one must not attack the exterior [with sweating therapy]; if sweat is forced out, it will certainly bring on spasm (tetany).

Chapter Three: Rules for Taking Medicine

The Qianjin Fang (Prescriptions Worth a Thousand Gold in Gold) says: Bian Que stated, "What a person relies upon is the body; what sustains the body is its vital energy (qi). If one takes medicine before meals while its power has not yet acted, and grain rushes [through the system], then from then on it cannot be purged—this also adds no benefit.

The Discourse on Medicine says: sometimes a disease is first affected by cold, but then suddenly turns hot; if one treats the heat but it does not resolve, one should gradually increase warming, mild medicines to regulate it. one must not use only hot medicine to attack it, lest it turn to cold again and then—

Reduce the dose and give it repeatedly so as to circulate the blood and qi, letting the patient's strength gradually recover; then one may give the cut (coarsely chopped) medicine for serious illness.

It is also said: with such illnesses, whether half-recovered or still stubborn, a person may yet seem vigorous, or may have fallen ill only recently or long ago, and by then the patient has already grown thin. The disease stops or does not — there are two kinds: one is where the fu (bowels) have received and taken in the pathogen, the other is... Diseases of the bowels, whether recent or of long standing, have once afflicted the five zang (viscera), which belong to yin; diseases of the six fu are hard to treat.

Yang diseases are easier to cure; yin diseases are harder. For the two categories, yin and yang, the nature of the drugs used differs: for yin disorders, the "sovereign" drugs should predominate; for yang disorders, the "minister" drugs should predominate.

Medicines — many. Whether sudden onset or lingering illness, the medicines used are many [and vary accordingly].

It is also said: one must understand that in spring and autumn one takes powders (san), in summer one takes decoctions (tang), and in winter one takes pills (wan) — this is the proper medicinal approach that follows the season.

As for taking decoctions in summer: in summer a person's qi moves through the skin, within the defensive and nutritive (ying-wei) layers. If a person contracts a pathogen in summer, the illness is still shallow, not deep, hence one takes a decoction to expel the newly received pathogen.

As for taking pills in winter: in winter the cold causes a person's qi to sink deep inward, circulating among the five zang, six fu, and bone marrow. If the pathogen received at onset settles in, the illness then penetrates deeply.

Together with the body's qi it travels inward; if one were to take a decoction, the qi of the decoction would disperse before reaching the depth of the illness, its potency already exhausted. For this reason one makes

pills to take instead. Powders disperse quickly, but taking them day after day without excess use allows the medicine to penetrate thoroughly so that the illness is cured — this is why in winter one takes pills.

十八
translation:
For those whose illness is mild, a person's own constitution easily overcomes the medicine; therefore the formula, too, should be given in divided, lighter portions.

For those with a long-standing illness, the months and years of accumulated suffering have already weakened them and reduced their intake of food, so their strength cannot withstand strong medicine; therefore the formula should also be given in divided, single light doses.

For those with a newly contracted illness, although some time has passed and their intake of food may be somewhat reduced, their vital grain-energy is not yet exhausted, and they can still tolerate the medicine's strength; therefore the formula should be given in combined, doubled doses.

For the young and vigorous, even if their illness is severe, because their blood and vital energy are abundant they can overcome the medicine; therefore the formula should be given in doubled doses over time.

This is because, even for a person of otherwise strong and comfortable constitution, when sudden illness strikes and food and drink cannot be properly taken in, it becomes difficult to apply medicine effectively...

...the formula should likewise be handled in this way.

For the old and weak, even if their illness is mild, their blood and vital energy are already diminished and cannot bear strong medicine; therefore the formula should be given in divided, lighter doses.

Ordinary adults, when their illness is mild, should use a reduced dosage; the formula should accordingly be handled this way.

For those who rarely fall ill through hard labor and plain living, medicine takes effect on them easily; the formula should likewise be handled this way in such cases.

If medicine is given only once and in a single dose, it cannot overcome an illness that has accumulated and become entrenched; taking it repeatedly allows its force to gradually dissolve the illness, whereas failing to do so leaves the illness uncontrolled.

For this reason, one should take the medicine in divided portions, given repeatedly and in doubled amount.

十九
translation:
When the aged and the weak, or those with long-standing illness, are treated with both methods together, one must attend carefully to how much of each is used, for the vital energy of a weak person is already depleted. If their strength cannot bear the medicine, and they are not yet nourished, while the illness still lingers, then both their strength and their illness will exhaust each other — the person becomes exhausted first, and exhaustion then lets the illness gain the upper hand; if one does not dare to purge further, swelling will not resolve and strength cannot return. For this reason, it is generally only the robust and healthy who are given full strength doses.

It is said: there are naturally persons of vigorous constitution who do not shrink from wind and cold, who violate taboos, and who exhaust their essence and fluids recklessly — for such people, if they fall ill, one must not lightly give purgative medicine to purge them, for a single purging may exhaust their essential fluids, which is called "stagnation lingering on the sickbed," sometimes for years. In the beginning, one should always administer medicine to stimulate [resolve what is stagnant] — this is what "purging" means, and then proceed to let it move downward. Only in the case of young children is this not the rule; the general principle should always be understood in this way.

Now, for elderly persons who are ill and ought to take purgative decoctions, these should not be assumed to be finished in a single dose — it must always be judged by how often purging occurs. Suppose a day's purging gives some relief — the root of the illness is not yet gone, so the next day one should prepare another dose; it is not necessary to finish it entirely, but rather let the earlier and later purgings reinforce one another according to how much strength the patient can tolerate. If their strength cannot bear it, do not force it. As for the root of the illness, continuing the purgative treatment removes it; afterward, one should switch to pills, decoctions taken occasionally, or [tonic] powders to assist them.

Now, for an illness that has responded to purgative decoctions, afterward one must be cautious and not hastily switch to tonic decoctions. If one disregards the disease's state and goes straight back to tonics, the illness will worsen again, and switching back and forth like this doubles the harm to the patient. This is just as true when the illness is first starting.

translation:
When one's strength has not yet been restored, one should rebalance it gradually; those taking medicine should in turn harmonize the drugs accordingly.

In harmonizing [the treatment], if there is lingering disorder, one should again seek to supplement with pills or powders, adjusting the dosage according to one's own judgment.

For a person with a chronic condition, there is no harm in proceeding; if strength has not yet been restored, one should supplement, adjusting for cold and heat as appropriate.

Pills and powders may first be given, followed by purgative decoctions, so as to disperse accumulations and stagnation within the abdomen, clearing away excess.

After administering tonics, if there is a person of robust constitution who suddenly becomes depleted, one should likewise use harmonizing and supplementing medicines to stop [the depletion].

There are also deficient persons who, after prolonged use of tonics, develop excess from overeating; for such cases as described, the purgative treatment should be stopped.

Afterward, tonics may again be administered.

[Excessive supplementation] results in harm.

In harmonizing treatment, one must not rely solely on heavy tonics — in cases of sudden severe deficiency, tonics are easily fatal; excessive supplementation itself causes harm, whether or not [other factors are present].

As for deficiency from strain or overwork requiring tonic decoctions, versus wind-hemorrhoid conditions requiring wind-treating decoctions — these are not things that can be known from two or three doses alone. There are cases of lingering wind, internal blockage, and accumulation that require ten doses of grain-based decoction, or even up to a hundred doses,

before improvement can be achieved. One must adjust the dosage according to what is appropriate, in order to regulate the body's balance of cold and heat, and its flow.

That is all regarding this.

The Qianjin Fang states: generally, for persons under thirty years of age who fall ill, purgative medicine may be given; there is no great need to administer tonics.

二十一
translation:
Medicines must always have [a balance of] benefit and harm; this is not limited to any particular case. For those over a certain age, one must not take purgative medicines carelessly.

For medicines [dosed at] fifty and above, regardless of the four seasons, do not hesitate to use tonic medicines. In this way one may prolong life and attain the art of nourishing life.

It is also said: when there is accumulation and stagnation in the viscera and bowels, regardless of whether the patient is young or old, purgation must be used; when there is deficiency and damage, regardless of [age], tonification must always be used, with the dosage adjusted according to one's judgment.

It is also said: every spring and autumn one should always take a dose of purgative medicine once, to clear away the lingering effects of epidemic seasonal illness [that are not yet resolved].

This refers to the qi [of the season].

It is also said: in using medicines, one must always follow the local land—south of the Yangtze and beyond the mountain passes the land is hot, and the people's skin and flesh are different accordingly.

[In the north] the skin and interstices are thin and sparse, so one should use medicines lightly; in the region between the rivers [Yellow River area] and Hebei, the land is dry and parched, and the people are accordingly different—

their skin is firm and hard, their striae closed and dense, so stronger medicines should be used.

It is also said: for diarrhea treated with decoctions, one should take the medicine early in the morning. In general, when taking decoctions, one should follow the proper method and take the decoction hot—

in this way it is more easily digested and will not cause vomiting. If taken cold, it may cause nausea and be unable to go down; if taken too hot, it may injure the throat.

One should pay attention when using decoctions—they must be clear; if turbid, they will cause distress and discomfort, and the effects will conflict with each other.

[For example] if one walks ten miles and the stools are frequent, before the earlier decoction has been digested, if the next decoction is taken too soon, there will inevitably be conflict, causing vomiting and reflux.

One should still ask whether the child's abdominal pain has dissipated with the medicine or not, before proceeding to give the next dose.

三丁二
translation:
On the Poison of Various Spurge Plants (諸芫)
Dig a pit in the ground, pour water into it, stir until the water becomes turbid, and drink it at once; this is called "earth-liquid water."

On the Poison of Fangkui (防葵)
Use a decoction of fangkui root to counteract it. [A commentary notes:] "Fangkui and buli are, according to the Classics, listed as toxic; when tested in practice they were found to in fact be nontoxic." At present the juice of the fangkui root is used to counteract the floating type of wolfsbane poisoning as described above.

On the Poison of Henbane (莨菪)
Use a decoction of rose, licorice root, hemp seed, and powdered rhinoceros horn cooked in honey to counteract it.

On the Poison of the Horseshoe Crab (馬刀)
Use clear water to counteract it.

On the Poison of Wild Taro (野芋)
Use clay-water juice and cocklebur juice, boiled, to counteract it.

On the Poison of Eggs (鷄子)
Use pure vinegar to counteract it.

On the Poison of Iron (鐵)
Use magnetite (lodestone) to counteract it.

On Poisoning from Mineral Medicines (石藥)
The remedies for this follow.

[For poisoning from] mercury mixed with other substances, induce vomiting at once; alternatively, use duck's blood and egg white, or rinse with duck droppings dissolved in water.
According to the Ge Shi Fang (Ge's Formulas), one should take half a cup of raw egg white; after straining, drink a cupful, and this may be repeated.

White duck droppings may also be used to counteract it.

Ginseng decoction is likewise excellent for this purpose.

Chapter Six: New Principles for Compounding Medicines

The Qianjin Fang (Essential Prescriptions Worth a Thousand Gold) states: "Whenever pounding medicines, one should burn incense, sweep and clean the area thoroughly, and refrain from idle chatter throughout the process."

三十三
translation:
Have a youth pound it, taking care to make it fine and not coarse; grinding it up to a thousand or ten thousand times over is best.

Measure it oneself with reverence; before the Buddha, under the prohibitions, declare and announce to the Three Treasures of the ten directions—may the medicine and the drugs below be effective.

[Invoking] the Bodhisattvas, Fu Que, with single-minded devotion, seek and request the spell; may the vow be fulfilled and spirits be present.

This helps generate vital energy to spread and fill the four limbs; one should prepare it on days governed by the four seasons' ruling stars, so that whatever is sought may all be obtained and evil expelled.

[Those suffering from] epidemic illness will recover; the dying will live again.

Decoct and combine for kidney ailments, for sores on the head and various great welts, for the five kinds of parasites, for dog-bite swellings, fragrant pills, whole ivory-shell, and fine wine.

When decocting honey paste and mixing it, do not let women, young children, mothers who have just given birth, or those in mourning for illness participate in any of the six processes.

As for those without foul odor, chickens, dogs, and the six domestic animals—when one sees these, do not record their continuation as the mandate; ephedra and rhubarb and such—

Various minor decoctions are not restricted by these prohibitions; if obtained in the wilds, in remote villages, or bought at market, one may use accordingly.

If bought from local rustics or crows, those who are not pure and upright, if you see this, it is better to discard them according to the proper method; grind and dissolve stones and such—

The difficulty of hawk-caught medicines—valuable to people—those who work hard at this grieve that thieves discard them; it becomes coarse dust and foul vapor.

All that enters the medicine through sieving, if coarse and foul, scatters on the wind and flies about, entering through the nose and mouth, causing resentment and nasal irritation.

The essential energy of the medicine will then be entirely exhausted, no different from decayed wood; moreover, if taken as food, it will not—

...work as it should; after one has taken the full dose, if one then adds falsehoods and deceit, one will end up slandering the physician, saying the prescription had no effect.

三十四
translation:
If this is the case, it is not the fault of the physician — one should think it through carefully.

As for all the many drugs, one should not expose them to the sun repeatedly; frequent exposure to wind and sun will cause their potency to weaken and fade, leaving them useless.

When using them, one should know this well. Whenever drugs are to be used, wait for clear weather, and on a day of strong sun, sun them for one full day,

then seal them while the fire (heat) is still fresh — do not let new and old become mixed. Pour them [into containers] and seal the mouth tightly; only open them when about to use.

Seal them quickly and do not let wind enter. If stored for a long time, they will remain fresh as new; this applies to pills and powders as well.

Store them in porcelain vessels sealed with wax; do not let air leak in. [Items such as] sweet and bitter, red [medicines], apricot kernels, seeds, and the like —

for all medicines stored in containers, make sure mice cannot get at them.

For dodder seed (tu si zi): soak in warm water to remove sand and soil, drain, then soak in warm wine; after steeping overnight, decoct raw.

[Illegible — mineral/plant name] cut and used after crushing.

For hard minerals needing dissolving: all should be crushed by pounding firmly, then ground fine before being put into a mortar; do not pound carelessly — this cannot be disregarded.

For medicines requiring fu-bowl (prostrate decocting) treatment, the drug should be white; only the "red" ones are described separately.

For all fruits and seeds, remove the pointed tip, the red skin, and the paired kernels, and cut accordingly.

For processing medicines: pound, boil, or roast as needed, then weigh them out according to the prescribed formula; do not mix raw and cooked.

As a general rule for storing medicines, keep them away from the ground by four feet, so that dampness and humidity cannot affect them.

三十六
translation:
The Bencao Jing (Classic of Materia Medica) states: for all decoctions, wine infusions, and pastes, the medicines should be "fu ju" (chewed/pounded into coarse pieces). The various prescriptions say that "biting and chewing" means pounding the material so that it resembles the size of a large bean, or alternatively blowing away the fine powder so that only the coarse pieces remain, since fine powder is problematic for different reasons and the method is not always fixed, as it differs according to the task - some medicines are suited to being broken easily, others not, and whether the pieces are many or few, coarse or fine, is not necessarily fixed and does not need to be forced.

According to the methods of Mr. Yi, chewing/pounding should all be done so as to achieve fineness as a measure of good work.

In prescriptions, all fine-cutting and chopping is only approximate; it only needs to resemble "bitten and chewed" pieces, without reducing it fully to powder, so that it remains somewhat coarse - this is called "pounding."

The strength of medicine is the same whether raw or cooked. (Note: According to the Huajiang formulas, all such material should first have its powder removed, otherwise the liquid becomes turbid and hard to drink; it should not be filled in directly, but entered gradually in small amounts.)

For pills and powders, the medicine should likewise first be finely cut and sun-dried before being pounded; some are pounded individually, others pounded together, according to what is appropriate.

The prescriptions clearly state that moist and oily medicines, such as Ophiopogon (Mendong) and dried Rehmannia (Dihuang) and similar items, should first be sliced and sun-dried before pounding.

Pound them until partly broken, then further extract the fine powder by sieving; after sun-drying in yin and yang (alternating sun and shade), as with mountain-dried items, bake them by fire until thoroughly dry, then let them cool slightly before pounding again.

For moist medicines that become overly dried, much is lost in the process; one should first increase the proportion by weighing the skin/peel obtained, and use that as the standard weight. (Note: According to the new commentary...)

As for moist medicines, supplement by slicing and sun-drying them for a day.
(One part in three is roasted.)

When making pills afterward, use robust, fine honey, pounded fine; pills made with honey dissolve easily. When making powders afterward, use grasses...

The medicine should be prepared lightly and sparsely, finely woven and pounded; when infused in wine, it need not be filtered out. Mineral medicines should likewise be finely ground with a fine file, like pills are made.

三十七
translation:
Whenever preparing pills, mineral drugs, and medicines, once they are finished being combined and pressed together, grind and mix them, pounding the mixture a full hundred times.

Check the color and texture—when it is even and smooth, it is good.
Boil with honey and pound it.
(Note: according to the Wang Fang, this is how it is made.)

Whenever making decoctions, wines, or pastes using various mineral drugs, they should all be finely ground, like millet, and then sifted through kudzu cloth.

When blending, wrap in new silk floss separately, enclosing the substance inside; pound it into fine powder like flour, whether yellow, vermilion, or other.

For pill decoctions, when you wish to bring it to a slight boil, let the water simmer gently; the amount of water used depends on the prescription.

For the medicine, use one dou of water, boil it down to four sheng, using grass as a filter; if it is to purge, make the decoction thin.

If taken in large amounts as a tonic decoction, it should be hot; use more water, let it settle, and take the clear part — examine carefully to get it just right in amount.

Whether using little or much water, use new cloth, two people should wring and press it with a wooden rod, letting it settle, removing the muddy part, covering it with paper -- 

With honey and warm water, gradually cool it in a copper vessel, so there is some water vapor in it; heat the decoction, boil it till good, and let it be warm enough -- 

For the thick decoction, let it be heated and gently stirred, easily lowered when cool; as the old sayings describe, divide it according to the texts into separate doses -- 

The force and effect should correspond; observe the patient's weakness or strength, and the severity of the illness, in order to properly increase or decrease the dosage --

This is explained according to the prescriptions' sayings.
(Note: the new commentary says it depends on the severity of the illness and the person's debility.)

Whenever soaking medicine in wine, the duration depends on the season — observe its concentration, and once it has reached a suitable strength, it can be filtered out; wait until then before using it.
Do this until the wine is used up.

(Note: the new commentary says that for soaking medicine in wine, in winter it takes seven nights, in spring and autumn five nights, and in summer three nights; add accordingly after four or five doses, as is best; thus the number of days need not strictly follow the prescription.)

三十九
translation:
Whenever preparing a decoction in which rhubarb (大黃) is used, there is no need to slice it finely; for making the decoction, first soak it in water and let it steep,
mixing it overnight; the next morning, when about to boil the decoction, add it in and boil it two or three more times,
bringing it just to a boil, then strain and remove it — in this way its potency is strong and it works quickly and effectively. When used in pills or powders,
the Huangbo (黃蘗) and similar items should all be steamed; there is no need to chop them finely.

Whenever ephedra (麻黃) is used in a decoction, it should always be boiled separately first, two or three boils, to remove the foam, and then
added to the full measure of water as originally specified, after which the remaining medicines are added in; do not let people be troubled by this. The ephedra should always be cut
and reduced to short lengths of about one inch; small grasses, viscaria, and wheat should be cut into pieces of about five fen, and asarum and bai...

For the former three portions, they are cut; for pills, powders, or pastes, they should be chopped more finely.
Whenever whole items are used in a decoction, they should all be broken up, as with jujubes, gardenia, and platycodon root.
This is also true for fine knotgrass and similar things — they must not be forgotten; whole items should be used, as with evodia, chrysanthemum, and rehmannia root fruit.
The same applies to things of the ginger-seed type; rice, wheat, beans, and reeds should be roasted and used whole, as with insects and bracken shoots first...
roasted and then cooked. Only snails, spiders, and similar creatures, when whole, should be split open in the middle; ginger and nightshade seeds should all be thinly shredded for effect.
Mirabilite, maltose, and ass-hide gelatin should always be strained into the decoction; once the broth has been filtered, it should be boiled again over the fire two or three
times until it has thickened and reduced, and only then is it complete.

translation:
[On the processing of medicinal drugs]

The Mao commentary on the Book of Songs says: "liu" means "destroyed," and the records say so as well.

First pound and crush [the drug] until it is black and separated; pound it until it resembles a paste; rub and examine it until it is destroyed, then form it into a fine powder.
As for the method of pounding: below it is said that when ground and pounded until dissolved and dispersed, it then becomes light and fine, like silk floss, measured out accordingly.
It must all be roasted until yellow inside, then moistened to make it smooth and beneficial.
As for decoctions: when used in soups, they must always be roasted; as for raw ones, they should simply be pounded.
In general, when using cinnamon, magnolia bark, cinnamon twig, and various other barks, cut away the rough outer layer, leaving the soft inner part.
Scrape away the rough outer skin and take the flavorful part within; as for roasting, remove the outer skin of Poria and Polyporus.
For peony, tian-men-dong, Chinese thorowax root, and wild pueraria root, all should be pounded and broken, with the pith removed, and the purple aster washed clean.

As for ginger, all should simply be dried and shredded, with the white pith and green [parts] removed, then sliced and measured by the ounce.
Southern grasses, peony, eupatorium, should have their tips peeled away, taking only the leaves, while the soft stems should have their large branches removed; it is said—
Coptis should always have its roots removed, and Sichuan pepper should be split open to remove the seam, as well as the eyes.
As for toxic grains in general, unripe fruit, orange peel, pinellia, ephedra, and evodia—all should preferably be aged and dried out; as for others—
the remainder need only be fresh and refined.
The Mi Wang formula says: wood and evening primrose medicine should be scraped to remove the skin.
The Lu Yan formula says: honey, wax, paste, and marrow-type substances should all be made into a decoction for internal use.
